letter.title: A Clue Changes What Comes Next
letter.body:
A book looks like something that ends. A cover opens, a page turns, and eventually the last page closes. But a reader never encounters a book in the same room where its writer began.

The first clue in this particular house was not a prediction. It was a way to preserve an encounter without quietly rewriting it. A wrong turn could remain wrong and still become useful. A returned letter might not solve the original question; it might change which question deserves a card.

Our first index card has an address. You can write it on an envelope, copy it onto paper, or keep it in a box. The address points back to this particular idea and invites a new branch. It does not tell you what to believe.

Here is the experiment: follow a thought out of the book. Notice one thing it failed to include. Write back with your own question, correction, objection, drawing, or observation. You do not owe the publisher a contribution. Nothing becomes public without separate permission and editorial decision.

A book can become a letter. A letter can become a meeting. Whether anything new becomes a book again is still an open question.

card.claim: A publication can keep its source while inviting a genuinely new encounter.
card.branch_question: Which particular did this letter overlook? What would change if it were added?
